title: NASA: This El Niño May Rival the 1997 Giant
paragraphs: NASA's Earth Observatory reports that the 2026 El Niño is developing so quickly that it may become as large as the powerful event of 1997–98. El Niño is a warming of the tropical Pacific that appears every two to seven years and changes rainfall patterns around the world.

The comparison is based on 35 years of satellite measurements of sea level. Nearly identical satellites, TOPEX/Poseidon in October 1997 and Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich in October 2026, show the same pattern: high, warm water pressing against South America. In 2015, by contrast, the warm water stayed farther offshore, so that strong event had different effects.

NOAA's outlook from 8 October 2026 gave an 83 percent chance of a strong to very strong El Niño in early 2027. However, this is a forecast, not a certainty. Effects far from the tropical Pacific are hard to predict, and the 1997 comparison only shows what could happen, not what will.

questions.q: Why is the 2026 El Niño unusual?
questions.a: It developed much faster than the one in 1997.

questions.q: What did the 2015 event look like?
questions.a: The warm water stayed farther offshore.

questions.q: Why should the forecast be read with care?
questions.a: Effects far from the Pacific are hard to predict.
